---
title: "License"
---

ferx is not under one license. Most of it is MIT; the model-search crate is
LGPL-3.0-or-later; and the `ferx` binary links both, plus third-party code.

## Which part is under which license

| Part | License | Where the text is |
|------|---------|-------------------|
| `ferx-core` (the engine) | MIT | `LICENSE` |
| `ferx-tools` (bootstrap, GAM screening) | MIT | `crates/ferx-tools/LICENSE` |
| `ferx-cli` source | MIT | `crates/ferx-cli/LICENSE` |
| `ferx-search` (modelsearch, covsearch, iivsearch, iovsearch, ruvsearch, allometry, amd, globalsearch) | LGPL-3.0-or-later | `crates/ferx-search/COPYING.LESSER`, `COPYING`, `NOTICE` |
| The `ferx` binary | MIT and LGPL parts, plus third-party notices | `ferx --licenses` |
| `data/mbma_naproxen.csv` (test data only) | CC BY-NC 4.0 | `data/mbma_naproxen.LICENSE` |

The root `LICENSE` file states the same split. Everything under
`crates/ferx-search` is LGPL, including its tests and test fixtures. The
scripts under `tools/pharmpy-*`, which run Pharmpy to produce those fixtures,
are MIT: they call Pharmpy as a program and contain none of its code.

### Why ferx-search is LGPL

The search tools follow the behaviour of
[Pharmpy](https://github.com/pharmpy/pharmpy) (LGPL-3.0-or-later), and parts of
them were written with its source as a reference. An audit found no copied
Pharmpy code, so the crate is ferx's own work, licensed to match. The crate's
`NOTICE` records this. The LGPL version 3 is a set of additional permissions on
top of the GNU GPL version 3, so the crate ships both texts.

`ferx-core` and `ferx-tools` never depend on `ferx-search`, so their source
stays MIT. You can use them, and embed them in your own software, under MIT
alone.

### Earlier releases stay MIT

The change is not retroactive. The model-search code was MIT-licensed while it
lived in `ferx-tools`, and every release of it up to and including
`ferx-tools` 0.4.0 remains MIT. `crates/ferx-search/LICENSE-MIT` reproduces that
license. The LGPL applies from 0.5.0, the first release of `ferx-search`.

Those earlier `ferx-tools` releases are not yanked from crates.io. Yanking would
not withdraw the MIT grant on code already published, and it would break builds
pinned to them.

## The ferx binary

`ferx` is built from all four crates. Its own source (`crates/ferx-cli`) is
MIT, but it statically links `ferx-search`, so a copy of the binary carries the
LGPL terms for that part. It also links the NLopt C library, whose Luksan
routines (including L-BFGS) are LGPL-2.1-or-later; the `nlopt` crate declares
only MIT, so crate metadata alone would miss this.

`ferx --licenses` prints everything a binary has to carry: the MIT license, the
LGPL-3.0 and GPL-3.0 texts, the `ferx-search` notice, how to rebuild the
binary, and the notices of every third-party crate it links. The third-party
part is generated from `Cargo.lock` by `tools/third-party-notices.py` into
`crates/ferx-cli/THIRD-PARTY-NOTICES.txt`; the `Licenses` CI job fails when it
is stale.

The R package (ferx-r) links `ferx-search` the same way and documents its own
notices.

## Rebuilding ferx with a modified ferx-search

The LGPL lets you replace the LGPL part of a binary with your own modified
version. Because Rust links statically, you do that by rebuilding from source.
The complete source of every released version is public:

- the git tag `vX.Y.Z` of
  [FeRx-NLME/ferx-core](https://github.com/FeRx-NLME/ferx-core), where `X.Y.Z`
  is the version `ferx --licenses` prints, and
- each crate on crates.io at that version.

To rebuild:

```bash
git clone https://github.com/FeRx-NLME/ferx-core
cd ferx-core
git checkout vX.Y.Z
# edit crates/ferx-search/...
cargo build --release --locked -p ferx-cli
```

The new binary is `target/release/ferx`. `--locked` keeps every other
dependency at the version the release used.
